correctness.rationale: For q even, the square map is a field automorphism, so the skew-polynomial quotient by the square of its variable is associative and local. Its units are the product of the square-zero radical units and the field units; a acts on 1+tε by t↦a⁻¹t. Inverting the complement parameter gives the affine action (the map is (t,a)↦(1+tε)a⁻¹). For odd q the translation subgroup K is self-centralizing. A normal 2-subgroup has trivial intersection with K, centralizes it, and is therefore trivial. The center of the affine group is trivial, forcing −1=1 in any realizing ring. In the finite ring the radical subgroup 1+J has 2-power order, so J=0. Artin–Wedderburn and scalar centers reduce the nontrivial factors to GL_d(F_2). The affine group is directly indecomposable: the minimal normal K is contained in one factor of any direct decomposition, as otherwise both factors would centralize it; the other factor then lies in K and is trivial. GL_d(F_2) is simple for d≥3 and cannot contain the proper normal K, while d=2 gives S_3 and q=3, which is realized by M_2(F_2). The trivial-complement case q=2 is included in the construction.
residual_risks: The nonrealizability argument requires finiteness; it does not address characteristic-zero realizing rings.

value.rationale: Scalar affine groups over all finite fields are a natural family in Fuchs' problem. The classification closes the extension-field gap rather than simply repeating the cyclic case, with a uniform explicit even-field realization and a characteristic/radical obstruction explaining exactly why odd extensions cannot occur.
residual_risks: No claim about higher affine degree, arbitrary complements, or infinite rings.
